articles.title: Specialist courts for rape cases to be rolled out in England and Wales
articles.summary: Funding will allow victims to view proceedings remotely and give evidence from a separate room via video link, the government says.
articles.content:
Specialist courts to handle cases of rape and other sexual offences will be introduced across England and Wales over the next two years, the prime minister has announced.

Each crown court will have at least one courtroom set up to hear such cases, while alleged victims will be able to view proceedings remotely and give evidence from a separate room via video link.

They will also be provided with private entrances and waiting rooms to separate them from defendants, though this will be dependent on the architecture of each building.

Rape Crisis England and Wales said this was a "significant step forward" that would introduce several reforms it had been requesting for years.

"Taken together, they reflect the urgency of ensuring that courts are fit for purpose and properly meet the needs of victims and survivors, which is crucial to securing justice," the charity's chief executive, Ciara Bergman, said.

Charities have complained that low prosecution rates for sexual offences and delays to court proceedings had disuaded victims from coming forward or pursuing justice.

Just 2.8% of rape offences recorded by police led to prosecutions in the year ending March 2024 and were the crimes that took the longest to investigate.

A prior ONS study, using data from 2017-2020, suggested that only a sixth of the actual number of rape and attempted rape victims had reported their assault to the police, with more than a third saying this was because they felt the police could not help or that the process would be humiliating.

Victims minister Alex Davies-Jones said the new measures were part of efforts to bring down a backlog of Crown Court cases, which stood at 80,098 at the end of March.

Rape Crisis England and Wales said 15,373 of these cases - 19% - related to sexual offences.

Davies-Jones told BBC Breakfast that the introduction of specialist courtrooms "isn't enough on its own" to tackle the backlog and stressed the importance of the Courts and Tribunals Bill to improve "timeliness, effectiveness and also prevention".

The Conservatives say the "long overdue" move should not come with restricting the number of jury trials, which is another provision of the bill.

Under the new measures, expected to cost around £23m of the Ministry of Justice's budget, court staff will also be given "trauma-informed training" and a single person of contact will be assigned to each survivor.

From next month, trials will be given a fixed date rather than placed on floating lists in what Prime Minister Andy Burnham said was an effort to "rebalance the scales of justice and put victims first".

There are 84 crown court buildings across England and Wales, containing around 500 courtrooms, and Davies-Jones said the government was determined that every one of them would have at least one specialist rape and sexual offences courtroom by 2028.

Where architecture might prevent courtroom upgrades, Davies-Jones said staff would be expected to co-ordinate a "trauma informed approach" - for instance by scheduling different arrival times and rooms to give evidence from for victims and defendants.

The government said the changes follow Labour MP Charlotte Nichols showing "immense strength and bravery" in speaking publicly about being raped and calling for changes to the justice system.

Nichols waived her automatic right to anonymity in March when she made a Commons speech in which she described having to wait more than 1,000 days to go to court.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on the introduction of specialist courts for rape and sexual offences in England and Wales, which will improve the justice process for victims by providing trauma-informed support, remote viewing and testimony options, and private facilities. This reform addresses significant issues of low prosecution rates and victim retraumatization, representing a meaningful and broad policy change with positive societal impact.
articles.personality_title: Specialist courts for rape cases to improve justice for victims in England and Wales
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In England and Wales, rape and sexual offence cases often face delays and low prosecution rates. Many victims feel the current court system is intimidating and does not support them well.

**What happened** – The government announced that over the next two years, every crown court will have at least one specialist courtroom for rape and sexual offence cases. Victims will be able to watch court proceedings remotely and give their evidence from a separate room using video links. Courts will also provide private entrances and waiting areas for victims to keep them separate from defendants, depending on the building's design. Court staff will receive training to better understand trauma, and each victim will have a single point of contact to guide them through the process.

**Impact** – These changes aim to make the justice system less stressful and more supportive for victims. By creating specialist courts and using technology, victims can avoid uncomfortable situations like facing defendants in person. This may encourage more victims to report crimes and help courts handle cases faster. The reforms respond to long-standing calls from charities and reflect a focus on fairness and care in sensitive cases.

**What's next step** – The government plans to have specialist courtrooms in all crown courts by 2028. Starting next month, trials will be scheduled on fixed dates to reduce delays. The Courts and Tribunals Bill will also work to improve the speed and fairness of court cases. Where building changes are difficult, courts will use other ways to support victims through careful scheduling and private spaces.

**One-sentence takeaway** – England and Wales are introducing specialist rape courts with new support measures to help victims give evidence safely and improve the justice process.
articles.personality_title_fr: Des tribunaux spécialisés pour les affaires de viol pour mieux soutenir les victimes en Angleterre et au Pays de Galles
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – En Angleterre et au Pays de Galles, les affaires de viol et d'agressions sexuelles connaissent souvent des retards et de faibles taux de poursuites. De nombreuses victimes trouvent que le système judiciaire actuel est intimidant et ne les soutient pas suffisamment.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Le gouvernement a annoncé que, dans les deux prochaines années, chaque couronne judiciaire disposera d'au moins une salle d'audience spécialisée pour les affaires de viol et d'agressions sexuelles. Les victimes pourront suivre les audiences à distance et témoigner depuis une pièce séparée grâce à des liens vidéo. Les tribunaux offriront aussi des entrées et salles d'attente privées pour les victimes afin de les séparer des accusés, selon la configuration des bâtiments. Le personnel judiciaire recevra une formation sur la prise en compte des traumatismes, et chaque victime aura un interlocuteur unique pour l'accompagner.

**Impact** – Ces changements visent à rendre le système judiciaire moins stressant et plus protecteur pour les victimes. En créant des tribunaux spécialisés et en utilisant la technologie, les victimes pourront éviter des situations difficiles comme se retrouver face à l'accusé. Cela pourrait encourager davantage de victimes à signaler les crimes et aider les tribunaux à traiter les affaires plus rapidement. Ces réformes répondent aux demandes des associations et montrent une volonté d'équité et de soutien dans ces dossiers sensibles.

**Prochaine étape** – Le gouvernement prévoit que tous les tribunaux de couronne aient une salle spécialisée d'ici 2028. Dès le mois prochain, les procès auront des dates fixes pour réduire les retards. Le projet de loi sur les tribunaux et les instances travaillera aussi à améliorer la rapidité et l'équité des procédures. Quand les changements de bâtiment sont difficiles, les tribunaux utiliseront d'autres méthodes comme la planification soignée et des espaces privés.

**Résumé en une phrase** – L'Angleterre et le Pays de Galles vont créer des tribunaux spécialisés pour les viols avec de nouvelles mesures pour aider les victimes à témoigner en toute sécurité et améliorer la justice.
articles.personality_title_es: Tribunales especializados para casos de violación mejorarán la justicia para víctimas en Inglaterra y Gales
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En Inglaterra y Gales, los casos de violación y delitos sexuales suelen enfrentar retrasos y pocas acusaciones. Muchas víctimas sienten que el sistema judicial actual es intimidante y no las apoya bien.

**Qué pasó** – El gobierno anunció que en los próximos dos años, cada tribunal de la corona tendrá al menos una sala especializada para casos de violación y delitos sexuales. Las víctimas podrán ver el proceso judicial a distancia y dar su testimonio desde una sala separada mediante videollamadas. Los tribunales también ofrecerán entradas y salas de espera privadas para las víctimas, separándolas de los acusados, según la estructura del edificio. El personal recibirá formación para entender mejor el trauma, y cada víctima tendrá un contacto único que la acompañará en el proceso.

**Impacto** – Estos cambios buscan hacer que el sistema judicial sea menos estresante y más comprensivo para las víctimas. Al crear tribunales especializados y usar tecnología, las víctimas evitarán situaciones incómodas como enfrentarse directamente a los acusados. Esto podría animar a más víctimas a denunciar y ayudar a que los casos se resuelvan más rápido. Las reformas responden a demandas de organizaciones y muestran un enfoque en la equidad y el cuidado.

**Próximo paso** – El gobierno quiere que para 2028 todos los tribunales tengan salas especializadas. Desde el próximo mes, los juicios tendrán fechas fijas para evitar demoras. La ley de tribunales también buscará mejorar la rapidez y justicia de los procesos. Cuando no sea posible cambiar los edificios, se usarán otras formas para apoyar a las víctimas, como horarios diferentes y espacios privados.

**Resumen en una frase** – Inglaterra y Gales están creando tribunales especializados para violación con nuevas medidas para ayudar a las víctimas a declarar con seguridad y mejorar la justicia.

articles.title: The right to development: Why equity, not charity, is a human right
articles.summary: Compare two children born in the same year: one in a country with functioning schools, social services, fair elections and a dynamic economy and the other in a nation devastated by poverty, conflict, climate change or corruption.
articles.content:
Neither chose their circumstances. Yet, one will likely live decades longer, earn far more and have a meaningful say in the decisions that shape their life.

The United Nations considers the gulf between those two children not simply unfair, but a violation of the right to development.

Since 1986, the UN has recognised development not merely as economic growth, but as a human right that belongs to us all.

It encompasses economic, social, cultural and political rights aimed at reducing inequality and creating a fairer world.

According to the World Inequality Report 2026, supported by the UN Development Programme (UNDP), half of the world’s poorest people own just two per cent of global wealth while the wealthiest 0.001 per cent – the billionaire class of around 56,000 people – hold three times more wealth than all of those poor people put together.

This is precisely the “widening inequality within and among countries” that the UN’s human rights office (OHCHR) says the right to development exists to confront.

© UNICEF/Shehzad Noorani

‘Inalienable human right’

The Declaration on the Right to Development (which is not a legally binding treaty) was agreed by UN Member States in 1986 and describes the “inalienable human right” to allow every person and people to “participate in, contribute to and enjoy” economic, social, cultural and political development.

Crucially, it includes people’s sovereignty over their own natural wealth and resources.

© UNICEF/Lisa Hill

Why does it matter?

The right to development “is not about charity, but enablement and empowerment”, the UN says.

Over the past 80 years since the end of the Second Word War, growth has not been shared equally and that inequality, left unaddressed, fuels poverty, unrest, migration and mistrust in institutions.

Key principles

People-centred development: The “human person” as subject and beneficiary of development

The “human person” as subject and beneficiary of development Participation: Active, free, meaningful involvement in decisions

Active, free, meaningful involvement in decisions Equity: Fair distribution of development’s benefits

Non-discrimination: No exclusion based on “race, sex, language or religion”

No exclusion based on “race, sex, language or religion” Self-determination: People should control their own resources

Do these principles really change lives?

Properly applied, the principles mean communities across the world do benefit.

In Morocco, vocational-training programmes are helping women launch income-generating activities.

Indigenous groups in Colombia have participated in the South American country’s peace accords.

In communities in Afghanistan, India and Palestine, people have learned how to share resources fairly rather than compete for them.

© FAO/Hashim Azizi

What happens when development leaves people behind?

The impact on people is just as concrete.

In Kenya, the Endorois, a community of roughly 60,000 people who had lived around Lake Bogoria for centuries, were excluded from the decision to turn their land into a game reserve. Denied consultation and a fair share of the reserve’s benefits, they lost the grazing pastures that were their livelihood, and large numbers of their cattle died.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, developing countries had less access to vaccines.

One UN official commented that “more than 600,000 deaths could have been prevented if all countries had been able to reach the World Health Organization vaccination target by the end of 2021. This failure was tragic and profoundly immoral.”

The barriers? Disagreement among States over binding obligations, weak international cooperation and a lack of political will are all holding back the right to development.

WHO

How relevant is it today?

Probably more relevant than ever before.

Climate shocks, conflict and immigration are overlapping global crises which are contributing to worsening poverty and inequality.

A fairer development system can help to reverse that trend.

Why is the UN focusing on this issue now?

It’s 40 years since the UN agreed on the 1986 Declaration on the Right to Development.

Member States will meet on 23 September at the UN in New York to renew the global commitment to ensuring that every person has a fair chance to live with dignity, opportunity and hope.

The meeting will bring together world leaders to reflect on progress made over the past four decades and to discuss how countries can work together to reduce poverty, expand opportunities and address inequalities that continue to prevent millions of people from fully benefiting from economic and social development.
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories
articles.reasoning: The article highlights the UN's recognition of the right to development as an inalienable human right aimed at reducing global inequality and empowering marginalized communities. It discusses concrete examples of positive impact and ongoing international efforts to renew commitment to equitable development, which has broad significance for millions worldwide.
articles.personality_title: UN renews focus on right to development as a key to fairness and opportunity
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The United Nations has recognized since 1986 that development is not just about economic growth but a human right. This right aims to ensure everyone, no matter where they are born, can take part in and benefit from fair social, economic, cultural, and political progress.

**What happened** – On September 23, 2026, UN Member States will meet in New York to renew their commitment to the right to development. This meeting marks 40 years since the original 1986 Declaration, and world leaders will discuss how to reduce poverty, fight inequality, and create more opportunities for people worldwide.

**Impact** – The right to development focuses on fairness and empowerment, not charity. It supports people’s control over their own resources and meaningful participation in decisions. Examples show this works: women in Morocco are starting businesses through training programs, Indigenous groups in Colombia are involved in peace efforts, and communities in Afghanistan, India, and Palestine are learning to share resources fairly. When development excludes people, like the Endorois community in Kenya losing access to their land, the results can be harmful and unfair.

**What's next step** – The upcoming UN meeting will review progress and seek stronger cooperation between countries to overcome current barriers such as political disagreements and weak international support. The goal is to create a fairer world where everyone has a chance to live with dignity and hope.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The UN’s renewed focus on the right to development aims to make fairness and opportunity real for all people by ensuring they can shape and share in their own growth.
articles.personality_title_fr: L’ONU renouvelle son engagement pour le droit au développement, clé de justice et d’opportunité
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Depuis 1986, l’Organisation des Nations Unies considère que le développement n’est pas seulement une croissance économique, mais un droit humain. Ce droit vise à garantir que chacun, où qu’il naisse, puisse participer et bénéficier d’un progrès social, économique, culturel et politique équitable.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Le 23 septembre 2026, les États membres de l’ONU se réuniront à New York pour renouveler leur engagement en faveur du droit au développement. Cette réunion marque les 40 ans de la Déclaration de 1986, et les dirigeants mondiaux discuteront de la réduction de la pauvreté, de la lutte contre les inégalités et de la création de plus d’opportunités pour tous.

**Impact** – Le droit au développement met l’accent sur l’équité et l’autonomisation, pas la charité. Il soutient le contrôle des ressources par les populations et leur participation aux décisions. Des exemples montrent son efficacité : des femmes au Maroc lancent des entreprises grâce à des formations, des groupes autochtones en Colombie participent aux accords de paix, et des communautés en Afghanistan, en Inde et en Palestine apprennent à partager les ressources équitablement. Quand le développement exclut, comme pour la communauté Endorois au Kenya privée de ses terres, les conséquences sont injustes et dommageables.

**Prochaine étape** – La réunion de l’ONU évaluera les progrès et cherchera à renforcer la coopération entre pays pour dépasser les obstacles actuels comme les désaccords politiques et le manque de soutien international. L’objectif est de construire un monde plus juste où chacun peut vivre avec dignité et espoir.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Le nouvel engagement de l’ONU pour le droit au développement vise à rendre réels la justice et les chances pour tous, en garantissant que chacun puisse façonner et partager sa propre croissance.
articles.personality_title_es: La ONU renueva su compromiso con el derecho al desarrollo como clave para la justicia y las oportunidades
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Desde 1986, las Naciones Unidas reconocen que el desarrollo no es solo crecimiento económico, sino un derecho humano. Este derecho busca que todas las personas, sin importar dónde nazcan, puedan participar y beneficiarse de un progreso social, económico, cultural y político justo.

**Qué pasó** – El 23 de septiembre de 2026, los Estados Miembros de la ONU se reunirán en Nueva York para renovar su compromiso con el derecho al desarrollo. Esta reunión celebra 40 años de la Declaración original y los líderes mundiales discutirán cómo reducir la pobreza, combatir la desigualdad y crear más oportunidades para todos.

**Impacto** – El derecho al desarrollo se centra en la equidad y el empoderamiento, no en la caridad. Apoya que las personas controlen sus recursos y participen en las decisiones. Ejemplos muestran que funciona: mujeres en Marruecos inician negocios con programas de formación, grupos indígenas en Colombia participan en acuerdos de paz, y comunidades en Afganistán, India y Palestina aprenden a compartir recursos de forma justa. Cuando el desarrollo excluye, como la comunidad Endorois en Kenia que perdió sus tierras, el daño es grave y desigual.

**Próximo paso** – La reunión de la ONU revisará los avances y buscará fortalecer la cooperación internacional para superar obstáculos como desacuerdos políticos y falta de apoyo. El objetivo es crear un mundo más justo donde todos puedan vivir con dignidad y esperanza.

**Resumen en una frase** – El renovado enfoque de la ONU en el derecho al desarrollo busca hacer realidad la justicia y las oportunidades para todas las personas, asegurando que puedan participar y compartir su propio crecimiento.
